question: What is the ratio loss in dynamic chunking and why is it needed?
gold: A loss that guides the fraction of selected boundaries toward a target compression ratio; without it the model could keep everything or compress too much
text:
Evidence: "Without explicit regularization, the model may converge to trivial solutions: either retaining nearly all vectors (negating computational benefits) or compressing excessively (losing critical information)." [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
Evidence: "we introduce a ratio loss to guide compression: 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) , 𝑁 −1 𝐹= 1 ∑︁ 𝑏𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1 𝐿 𝐺= 1 ∑︁ 𝑝𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1" [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
Evidence: "When 𝐹 = 𝐺, the loss attains a minimum of Lratio = 1 when 𝐹 = 𝐺 = 𝑁1 ." [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
The ratio loss is an auxiliary loss that penalizes deviations from a target compression ratio 𝑁, defined as 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) . [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
It is needed because, without it, the model could either keep almost all vectors or compress too much, harming performance . [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
The loss drives the model toward the desired ratio by aligning the fraction of selected vectors 𝐹 with the average boundary probability 𝐺, reaching a minimum when 𝐹 = 𝐺 = 𝑁1 . [HNET §2.2.3 Ratio Loss, p.8]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "Without explicit regularization, the model may converge to trivial solutions: either retaining nearly all vectors (negating computational benefits) or compressing excessively (losing critical information)."  
Q2 [C1] "we introduce a ratio loss to guide compression: 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) , 𝑁 −1 𝐹= 1 ∑︁ 𝑏𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1 𝐿 𝐺= 1 ∑︁ 𝑝𝑡 , 𝐿 𝑡 =1"  
Q3 [C1] "When 𝐹 = 𝐺, the loss attains a minimum of Lratio = 1 when 𝐹 = 𝐺 = 𝑁1 ."

ANSWER: The ratio loss is an auxiliary loss that penalizes deviations from a target compression ratio 𝑁, defined as 𝐿 Lratio = 𝑁 ((𝑁 − 1)𝐹𝐺 + (1 − 𝐹 ) (1 − 𝐺)) [Q2]. It is needed because, without it, the model could either keep almost all vectors or compress too much, harming performance [Q1]. The loss drives the model toward the desired ratio by aligning the fraction of selected vectors 𝐹 with the average boundary probability 𝐺, reaching a minimum when 𝐹 = 𝐺 = 𝑁1 [Q3].

question: Why did the authors of Attention Is All You Need choose sinusoidal positional encodings over learned ones?
gold: Both gave nearly identical results; sinusoidal may let the model extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than seen in training
text:
Evidence: "We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos ." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
Evidence: "We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
Evidence: "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training." [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they hypothesize it would let the model learn relative positions easily, as offsets become linear functions of the encodings . [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
They also found that learned embeddings gave nearly identical results, but preferred the sinusoidal form for its potential to extrapolate to longer sequences . [ATT §3.5 O(n2 · d), p.6]
raw:
ANSWERABLE: yes  
Q1 [C1] "We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos ."  
Q2 [C1] "We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E))."  
Q3 [C1] "We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training."  

ANSWER: The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they hypothesize it would let the model learn relative positions easily, as offsets become linear functions of the encodings [Q1]. They also found that learned embeddings gave nearly identical results, but preferred the sinusoidal form for its potential to extrapolate to longer sequences [Q2][Q3].

question: What does the smoothing module in H-Net do?
gold: Interpolates/de-chunks representations with an exponential moving average weighted by the router's boundary probabilities, making the discrete chunking trainable
text:
Evidence: "The smoothing module applies an exponential moving average (EMA) with the following definition: 𝑧¯𝑡 = 𝑃𝑡 𝑧ˆ𝑡 + (1 − 𝑃𝑡 )𝑧¯𝑡 −1 ." [HNET §2.2.2 Dechunking, p.7]
Evidence: "By smoothly interpolating between discrete choices based on confidence scores, a smoothing module prevents the model from overfitting to suboptimal chunking patterns early in training." [HNET §2.2.2 Dechunking, p.7]
Evidence: "The dechunking layer (Dechunk in equation (3)) consists of a smoothing module and upsampler, as illustrated in Figure 1( top-right )." [HNET §2.2.2 Dechunking, p.6]
The smoothing module converts discrete chunk boundaries into a continuous representation by applying an exponential moving average of the upsampled vectors weighted by boundary confidence, enabling differentiable back‑propagation through chunk boundaries. [HNET §2.2.2 Dechunking, p.7]
It also smooths low‑confidence chunks with previous context, correcting misalignments and improving training stability . [HNET §2.2.2 Dechunking, p.6; HNET §2.2.2 Dechunking, p.7]

ANSWER: The smoothing module converts discrete chunk boundaries into a continuous representation by applying an exponential moving average of the upsampled vectors weighted by boundary confidence, enabling differentiable back‑propagation through chunk boundaries.
